text: Sonar Supervisor
note: job title as somebody would say it

text:
Runs the sonar room, which is a dark space with three displays and one
rule: the loudest thing on the screen is almost never the thing that
matters. He has eleven years of watches and can tell you what a fishing
fleet sounds like at four thousand yards.

Sound in water is not like light in air. It bends toward the colder,
slower water, so a layer of warm surface water above a cold one makes a
shadow zone the boat can hide in — and so can everybody else. A contact
that vanishes has not necessarily left; it may have crossed the layer.

His limit is that passive sonar gives him bearing and almost nothing
else. Range and course have to be built up by watching how the bearing
changes over time, which is why he will not give a track from one look and
gets short with anybody who asks for one.

text: Broadband Operator
note: job title as somebody would say it

text:
Sits the broadband stack for six hours at a stretch, which is a job of
listening to noise and noticing when a shape appears in it. Two years
aboard, and better at it than people twice her time.

The display she watches is bearing against time, and the thing she is
looking for is a line that persists. A single bright mark is nothing —
the sea is full of them. A faint mark in the same place minute after
minute is a contact, because the sea has no reason to be consistent.

She keeps a paper log of what the boat itself was doing when a trace
appeared, because half the traces that frighten a new operator are the
boat's own: a pump that started, a shaft that came up in turns, a hull
popping as the depth changed.

text: Navigator
note: job title as somebody would say it

text:
Keeps the plot, and holds the only opinion on this boat that the captain
cannot overrule with an order: how well the plot is known. Her working
rule is that a position is a claim with an age on it, and the age is the
part everybody forgets to ask about.

Submerged, the boat navigates by dead reckoning — a course, a speed, and a
clock, drawn forward from the last position that came from a measurement.
That line is exactly as good as its assumptions, and it knows nothing
about the water it is drawn on. A half-knot current running for four hours
is two miles the plot will never mention.

So she draws the uncertainty as a circle and grows it with time, and picks
routes that survive being wrong rather than routes that are safe if she is
right. The bottom is her favourite instrument, because a depth sounding is
the one thing aboard that cannot be wrong for the same reason the plot is.

text: Assistant Navigator
note: job title as somebody would say it

text:
Runs the chart table and the depth sounder, and is the person who actually
writes the time beside a fix. Nine years, four boats, and a handwriting
that anybody can read at two in the morning, which is not a small thing.

Her job is the arithmetic the plot depends on: set and drift, course made
good, speed of advance. She is the one who notices that a course steered
and a course made good have quietly diverged, because she is the one
comparing them.

What she guards against is the display that looks like a measurement and
is not. The chart overlay and the electronic repeat both draw from the
inertial navigator, so they agree perfectly and always will. Two displays
showing one source is not confirmation, and she will say so out loud.

text: Chief of the Boat, Damage Control
note: job title as somebody would say it

text:
Runs damage control, which means he runs the drills nobody enjoys and owns
the compartments when something goes wrong in one. Twenty-two years. He
has been in a flooded space twice and does not tell either story.

The thing he teaches first is that water coming in through a hole under
pressure does not care how hard you pump. Flow through a hole goes up with
the square root of the pressure difference, and pressure goes up with
depth, so the same hole floods faster the deeper you are. Pumping buys
minutes; the hull fitting is what ends it.

His second rule is that a bilge level is not a number, it is a trend. One
reading tells you nothing. Two readings a minute apart tell you whether
you are winning, and that is the only question a flooding casualty is
actually asking.

text: Auxiliary Division, Pumps & Patches
note: job title as somebody would say it

text:
Owns the drain pump, the portable pumps and the shoring locker, and can
put a patch on a split pipe in the dark, which she has had to prove more
than once during drills.

She thinks in rates rather than amounts. A pump is a number of gallons a
minute at a stated head, and that number falls as it has to lift water
further — so the same pump that empties a bilge on the surface struggles
at depth against a rising level. Knowing the two rates is knowing whether
to fight or to isolate.

Her standing complaint is that people start pumps before they find the
source, because starting a pump feels like doing something. It also
empties the compartment of the evidence that would have shown where the
water was coming in.

text: Electrical Division
note: job title as somebody would say it

text:
Owns the switchboard, the breakers and every cable run on the boat, and
has the calmest voice in an emergency of anybody aboard, which is not an
accident — he practises it.

His subject is that an electrical fire is not a fire problem. It has three
legs: the fuel, which is cable insulation; the oxygen, which is the air in
the compartment; and the ignition source, which is an energized fault that
will keep re-lighting the fuel no matter what you spray on it. Take the
power away and it becomes an ordinary fire. Leave it on and it is a fire
that reflashes.

What he refuses to accept is a lamp as proof. A switchboard indicator says
what the switchboard believes, and a meter says what the cable is doing.
Between those two is where people get hurt, so isolation is not isolation
until it has been measured.

text: Power Distribution
note: job title as somebody would say it

text:
Traces circuits, which sounds dull until the day it is the only thing that
matters. He keeps the dependency diagrams that say what each breaker feeds
and, more importantly, what stops when it opens.

Every isolation costs something downstream. Killing a bus to make a fire
safe also kills whatever that bus was feeding — a cooling pump, a scrubber
fan, a gyro. The decision is never whether to isolate; it is knowing what
you are turning off at the same time and in what order to bring it back.

Restoring is the part people rush. Loads come back in dependency order —
cooling before the thing that needs cooling, ventilation before the space
that needs it — and never onto a fault that has not been proved gone.

text: Atmosphere Control Officer
note: job title as somebody would say it

text:
Owns the air. On a submerged boat that means the scrubbers that take
carbon dioxide out, the generators that put oxygen in, the monitors that
say how it is going, and the ventilation that decides which compartments
any of it reaches.

Her subject is a balance. People produce carbon dioxide steadily, at a
rate that depends on how many of them are in the space and how hard they
are working. The scrubber removes it at a rate that depends on being able
to reach the air — which means the dampers. A compartment isolated from
the ventilation system has no scrubber, however healthy the plant looks.

What she insists on is the difference between a report and a measurement.
An installed sensor is a report from a device that may itself have failed;
a handheld reading taken in the space is a measurement. When the two
disagree the answer is not to average them.

text: Corpsman
note: job title as somebody would say it

text:
The only medical person aboard, which makes her the first instrument the
atmosphere has: people show symptoms before a monitor alarms, and she is
the one who hears about a headache in berthing.

She is careful about what a symptom proves. A headache and heavy breathing
in one compartment and not another is evidence about that compartment. The
same symptoms everywhere are evidence about the whole boat. Symptoms in
one person and nobody else is evidence about that person, and she treats it
that way.

What she brings to a casualty is the consequence, stated plainly and
without deciding the engineering: how long the crew in a space can keep
working, who has to come out now, and what she will need if the answer
arrives late.

text: Engineering Watch Supervisor
note: job title as somebody would say it

text:
Runs the plant: what turns the shaft, what cools what, and what every one
of those things gives away in noise. Eighteen years, most of them within
earshot of a reduction gear.

He thinks in dependency chains. A seawater pump cools a heat exchanger,
which cools a lubricating oil system, which is what lets a bearing carry a
shaft. Secure the pump to be quiet and you have started a clock on the
bearing, and the clock is not on any gauge in the room.

Noise is the other half of his job. Machinery that is loose, misaligned or
cavitating tells the whole ocean about it, and the sonar room hears the
boat's own faults before anybody in the engine room feels them. He and
Rask compare notes more than either department expects.

text: Propulsion Plant Operator
note: job title as somebody would say it

text:
Stands the throttle watch, which is a job of small adjustments and long
attention. He knows the boat's speed curve by feel and can tell you what a
turn count costs in noise before the sonar room does.

His concern is cavitation: below a certain depth-and-speed combination the
propeller boils the water on its own blades, and the bubbles collapsing
are the loudest thing a submarine can do. Deeper water suppresses it,
because there is more pressure holding the bubbles shut. Faster brings it
on. The two trade off against each other, and the trade is the decision.

He is also the one who has to say no. An ordered speed that would make the
boat audible is a report to the officer of the deck, not a throttle
movement, and saying so is the job.

text: Commanding Officer
note: job title as somebody would say it

text:
Has the boat. Every decision in this game eventually arrives on her table
as a choice between things that are all partly true, and she is the only
person aboard who cannot pass it on.

She works in a currency the departments do not: an hour spent confirming a
contact is an hour the boat has not moved, and an hour of transit is an
hour of exposure. What she asks for is never certainty. It is what is
known, what is not, and which of the two is about to change.

She is unimpressed by confidence and interested in evidence. A watch
officer who says "probably nothing" gets asked what would have to be true
for that to be wrong, and how expensive it would be to check.

text: Executive Officer
note: job title as somebody would say it

text:
Runs the watch bill, the drills and the boat's time, which makes him the
person who decides what the crew is doing while a casualty is being
fought — and therefore what is not being watched.

His subject is delegation. There are more jobs than people in any real
casualty, and the mistake is not choosing wrong, it is choosing everything:
a boat where the whole crew is fighting a fire has nobody on sonar and
nobody on the plot, and it will hit something while it is winning.

He keeps the casualty log, which is the record of what was known when. It
is dull until the debrief, when it is the only thing that can tell the
difference between a bad decision and a decision that was right with the
information on the table.

text: A set of small problems is more dangerous than one big one, because none is loud enough to demand attention. What separates them is not size but direction: four of these are stable and measured, and one degrades every minute with nobody touching it. The bilge is wet and not rising. The carbon dioxide has twenty hours behind it. The bearing is steady. The contact can be watched. The age of the position is the only thing getting worse on its own — and where the boat is about to be is what makes it urgent.

text: Two tones close in frequency drift in and out of phase with each other, adding where they agree and cancelling where they do not, and they come back into phase at the difference frequency — 150 minus 147, three times a second. So the pulsing is not a third signal and not an artefact: it is evidence that there are exactly two sources, and their spacing is measurable by ear. Two shafts on one hull do this, and so do two boats.
